items.explanation: Plains diaries stress mutual aid — barn raisings, shared wells, cooperative threshing — because no isolated family could survive drought, blizzards, and grasshopper plagues alone.
options: A. Arrived as single men without families
B. Applied farming methods learned in the East
C. Embodied rugged individualism
D. Depended on help from neighboring settlers
items.stem: Farmers who succeeded on the Great Plains

option_explanations.A: The opposite of the pattern. Plains families needed everyone — men, women, and children — working the farm together; a lone man without a family was the least likely to succeed, not the most.
option_explanations.B: Eastern farming methods often failed on the Plains — the climate was drier, the soil tougher, and crops that thrived in Ohio or Pennsylvania withered. Successful farmers had to adopt new techniques (dry farming, deep plowing, hardy wheat varieties), not copy Eastern practices.
option_explanations.C: Rugged individualism is the myth, not the reality. Diaries of Plains settlers stress mutual aid — barn raisings, shared wells, cooperative threshing — because no isolated family could survive drought, blizzards, and grasshopper plagues alone.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Successful Plains farmers depended on help from neighbors — shared labor, equipment, and knowledge — because the environment was too harsh for any single family to manage on its own.

items.explanation: In 1879 thousands of Southern Blacks fled to Kansas, naming themselves for the biblical Exodus from Egypt.
options: A. Miners newly arrived in Oregon
B. Southern Blacks who migrated west to farm
C. Laborers who cleaned grain on bonanza farms
D. Immigrants who headed west to farm

option_explanations.A: Exodusters were not miners, and they did not head to Oregon. They were Southern Black farmers fleeing to Kansas, not prospectors in the Pacific Northwest.
option_explanations.B: Correct. In 1879 thousands of formerly enslaved Southern Blacks fled to Kansas — naming themselves for the biblical Exodus from Egypt — to escape violence and sharecropping and farm land of their own.
option_explanations.C: Bonanza farms were giant wheat operations in the Dakotas worked by hired labor, but the people who worked them were not called Exodusters. The Exodusters were Southern Black migrants to Kansas.
option_explanations.D: Exodusters were not immigrants — they were native-born Americans, mostly formerly enslaved Southern Blacks. Immigration refers to people arriving from other countries.

items.explanation: The 1887 act allotted reservation land to individual Native families to make them farmers, 'civilizing' them by breaking up tribal holdings — with 'surplus' land sold to whites.
options: A. Sought to turn Native Americans into individual farmers
B. Shielded Native land from further white encroachment
C. Split large reservations into smaller ones
D. Outlawed the Ghost Dance

option_explanations.A: Correct. The 1887 Dawes Act divided reservations into individual allotments, aiming to turn Native Americans into small farmers — the government's plan to 'civilize' them by breaking up tribal landholding, with leftover 'surplus' land sold to white settlers.
option_explanations.B: The opposite of what happened. The Dawes Act stripped roughly two-thirds of Native-held land, much of it bought by white settlers; it accelerated white encroachment, not shielded against it.
option_explanations.C: The Dawes Act did not create smaller reservations — it carved individual family allotments out of existing reservations, dissolving the reservation itself as a tribal holding and selling the remainder.
option_explanations.D: The Ghost Dance was suppressed by military force at Wounded Knee in 1890, not outlawed by the Dawes Act, which dealt with land allotment, not religion.

items.explanation: The Grange and Farmers' Alliances organized farmers, but the Populist (People's) Party carried their demands — free silver, railroad regulation, graduated income tax — to a national audience in 1892.
options: A. Greenback Party
B. Populist Party
C. The Grange
D. Farmers' Alliances
items.stem: The organization that gave farmers' views the largest national audience was the

option_explanations.A: The Greenback Party did give farmers an early political vehicle in the 1870s, but it was a short-lived currency-focused party — it never carried farm demands to as large a national audience as the Populists did in 1892.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The Grange and Farmers' Alliances organized farmers locally, but the Populist (People's) Party carried their platform — free silver, railroad regulation, a graduated income tax — into a national presidential campaign in 1892, giving farm views their largest national audience.
option_explanations.C: The Grange organized farmers socially and politically and won state railroad laws, but it stayed out of national electoral politics — its reach was regional, not the national platform the Populists built.
option_explanations.D: The Farmers' Alliances built huge membership rolls and fed directly into the Populist Party, but as organizations they were the farm movement's base; it was the Populist Party's presidential campaign that put their demands before the whole nation.

items.explanation: Turner's 1893 frontier thesis argued that the westward-moving frontier forged American democracy and individualism — though he later admitted he had ignored the Native peoples destroyed by it.
options: A. Echoed dime novels' romantic view of the West
B. Reckoned with the massacre of Native Americans
C. Stressed western expansion's effect on the American character
D. Emphasized the hardships of frontier settlements

option_explanations.A: Turner's thesis was a scholarly argument, not a dime novel. It did not romanticize the West — it claimed the frontier had shaped the national character, a very different kind of claim from adventure fiction.
option_explanations.B: Turner's 1893 thesis notably did not reckon with the destruction of Native Americans — he treated the frontier as empty land meeting settlers. He only later admitted he had ignored the Native peoples destroyed by expansion.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Turner's 1893 frontier thesis argued that the westward-moving frontier — the meeting of settlers with open land — forged American democracy, individualism, and character. The thesis is about what expansion did to Americans, not about the West's hardships.
option_explanations.D: Turner did not dwell on frontier hardships. His argument was about the frontier's effect on American character and institutions — democracy and individualism — not about how difficult settlement was.

items.explanation: Congress granted railroads millions of acres because the lines would bind the nation and fill the West with settlers — the Pacific Railway Acts of the 1860s.
options: A. It wanted to promote western settlement
B. It needed to move troops during the Civil War
C. Senators wanted to aid steel-industry backers
D. Politicians hoped to relieve unemployment
items.stem: The federal government subsidized the transcontinental railroad with lavish land grants because
items.stimulus:
Questions 6–8 refer to the illustration described below.

The famous 1869 photograph of the Golden Spike ceremony at Promontory Summit, Utah: two locomotives face each other, their cowcatchers nearly touching, while railroad workers, officials, and a military band crowd around the tracks where the final spike joins the Union Pacific and Central Pacific lines.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Congress poured land grants into the transcontinental railroads under the Pacific Railway Acts because the lines would bind the nation together and fill the West with settlers — settlement was the whole purpose of the subsidy.
option_explanations.B: Wrong war and wrong reason. The transcontinental line was authorized during the Civil War (1862) but finished in 1869, and it was not built to move troops — its purpose was binding the country and opening the West.
option_explanations.C: Steel interests certainly profited from railroad construction, but senators did not vote land grants to enrich them — the grants were about national expansion and settlement, not industrial favors.
option_explanations.D: Unemployment relief was not a 1860s rationale for rail subsidies; large-scale federal job-creation policy did not exist until the Depression-era 1930s. The grants were about settlement and national unity.

items.explanation: Between 1865 and 1890 railroads, mining, cattle, and farming overran the region; Native nations were confined to reservations and the Census Bureau declared the frontier closed in 1890.
options: A. The West stayed largely unexplored wilderness
B. The frontier rapidly disappeared
C. The U.S. seized new lands from Mexico and Britain
D. The West became a manufacturing center
items.stem: Which best describes the West in the 25 years after the Civil War?
items.stimulus:
Questions 6–8 refer to the illustration described below.

The famous 1869 photograph of the Golden Spike ceremony at Promontory Summit, Utah: two locomotives face each other, their cowcatchers nearly touching, while railroad workers, officials, and a military band crowd around the tracks where the final spike joins the Union Pacific and Central Pacific lines.

option_explanations.A: By the 1890 Census the West was thoroughly mapped, railroaded, mined, and settled — the Census Bureau itself declared the frontier closed in 1890. 'Unexplored wilderness' describes the early 1800s, not the post–Civil War quarter century.
option_explanations.B: Correct. In the 25 years after the Civil War, railroads, mining, cattle ranching, and farming overran the West, Native nations were confined to reservations, and the Census Bureau declared the frontier closed in 1890.
option_explanations.C: No new lands were seized from Mexico or Britain after the Civil War. The last major acquisitions — the Mexican Cession, the Gadsden Purchase, Alaska (1867) — were already made; the postwar story was settlement, not conquest.
option_explanations.D: The West produced minerals, cattle, timber, and wheat — extractive goods shipped east and abroad. Manufacturing stayed concentrated in the Northeast and Midwest; the West did not become a manufacturing center.

items.explanation: Farmers needed the railroads to reach markets but hated the freight rates the lines charged — rates set by monopolies that could make or break a harvest's profit.
options: A. Railroads could seize farmland by eminent domain
B. Railroads favored cattle ranchers
C. Railroads brought immigrant waves to their lands
D. Railroads controlled farm profits through freight rates
items.stem: Farmers prized railroad access but feared the railroads because
items.stimulus:
Questions 6–8 refer to the illustration described below.

The famous 1869 photograph of the Golden Spike ceremony at Promontory Summit, Utah: two locomotives face each other, their cowcatchers nearly touching, while railroad workers, officials, and a military band crowd around the tracks where the final spike joins the Union Pacific and Central Pacific lines.

option_explanations.A: Eminent domain was not the farmers' grievance. Railroads already owned their corridors and vast land grants — what farmers feared was economic, not the seizure of their land.
option_explanations.B: Cattle ranchers depended on the railroads too, but farmers' anger was not about favoritism toward ranchers. Their complaint was about the freight rates charged to them.
option_explanations.C: Immigrants did arrive by rail, but farmers did not fear the railroads for carrying people — they feared them for controlling the cost of shipping their crops to market.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Farmers needed railroads to reach markets, but the lines were often monopolies that set freight rates high enough to swallow a harvest's profit — so the railroad decided whether a farmer made money or not.
